Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.research_questions:
We investigate young children’s comprehension of deictic reference in the graphic domain. Two-, three-, and four-year-old children are presented with an object-choice-task in which a cartoon agent is providing cues to help participants choose between two options presented at the left and right bottom of the screen. The cues are triangle cues placed in four positions between the choice options. Two of the positions are closer to either choice option. Triangle cues are either pointing to the nearest target (congruent condition, i.e. distance and direction align) or pointing in the opposite direction (incongruent conditions, i.e. distance and direction are in conflict).
We code as correct when children choose the option that the triangles are pointing to. We are using age as continuous predictor in a within-subjects design (congruent; incongruent) and investigate when children’s group performance deviates from chance level in either condition. We hypothesize that (1) children will succeed earlier in the congruent than in the incongruent condition and that (2) in the incongruent condition, younger children will prefer the target closest to the cue whereas older children will prefer the target that the cue is pointing to.
table.design_dependent_variables: The key dependent variable is children’s choice behavior in the object-choice-task. Choice items are presented on the left and right side of the screen. Children respond by pointing to the side of their choice. Children’s choices are coded as correct (1) or incorrect (0). We code as correct when children choose the option that the triangles are pointing to.
table.study_design_overview: In a within-subjects design, children will be presented with an equal number of trials of the congruent and incongruent condition.
table.statistical_tests:
All analyses will be computed in R (R Core Team, 2018). Bayesian models will be run in Stan (http://mc-stan.org/) and implemented via the function brm of the package brms (Bürkner, 2017). We will use logistic Bayesian generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) to fit children’s responses (0/1) as a function of their absolute age in days, task (congruent, incongruent) and an interaction between trial and task. We use default priors and include trial and sex as fixed effects to be controlled for. Trial number will be added as a random slope within subject.
Model: correct ~ task*z.age +z.trial +z.sex +(z.trial|id)
•	correct: correct choice (0/1); 
•	task: congruent condition or incongruent condition; 
•	z.age: age in days, centered to a mean of 0 
•	z.trial: trial number, scaled
•	z.sex: participants’ sex (male/female), scaled
•	id: participant id
The analysis will model participants binary choices to predict the probability of children interpreting the cues correctly and model how this probability will change as a function of their absolute age in days. In order to evaluate the relevance of age and task type for children’s performance, we will compare a full model as specified above with a reduced model lacking the interaction of age and task by using WAIC scores and weights (McElreath, 2016). Furthermore, we will inspect the model estimates for the different predictors (including their 95% Credible Interval (CrI)). In addition, we use the model to predict the developmental trajectory (with 95% CrI) for each task type. The criterion for settling when children perform above chance with either type of stimuli is the point at which the  95% CrI for a particular trajectory does no longer overlap with a midline demarcating the 50% chance level.
To further explore our data, we also bin participants by year of age. To test whether group-level performance is above chance in all age groups, we use two-tailed one-sample t-tests with the chance level set to .5. We provide Cohen's d as a standardized effect size for significance testing (computed via the function `cohensD`). Additionally, each participant's data will also be submitted to a binomial test to determine whether their performance is above chance on an individual level.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Prior to the main study phase, children are tested with familiarization trials in which they simply have to point to the position of an item that was hidden in plain sight. This serves to ensure that children are comfortable and understand the search game.
In order to enter the main study phase, children should have a success rate of 66% in the familiarization. The experimenter provides at least four trials. If three in four are correct (75%), the child proceeds to the main phase. If not, two additional familiarization trials are run. If the child is correct in four out of six trials (66%), she proceeds to the main study phase. If not, two additional trials are presented. If six in eight are correct (75%), the child enters the main study phase. If children do not fulfill the criterion in a maximum of eight trials, they are dropped from the sample. 
Children will also be excluded from the sample if they do not provide at least eight valid out of 16 possible trials in the main study phase. Trials are excluded if children do not respond, if responses cannot be interpreted, if parents or caregivers interfere with the procedure, or on the basis of technical problems or experimenter error.
table.sample_size: Starting at 24 months, we will test two children per month over an age-range of 36 months for a total sample of 72 children. Each child contributes a minimum of eight and a maximum of 16 trials. While using age as a continuous predictor is rare in developmental studies, we aim at having a sample of at least 24 children per year of age (two-, three-, and four-year-olds) which is in line with conventions in the field. In case children in either condition do not perform above chance as a group within the current age-range, the age-range will be extended by a year increasing the sample by 24 children until performance surpasses chance-level.
table.additional_comments:
Data collection for the main sample began in July 2021 and is nearly complete by the time of preregistration. Therefore, this preregistration mainly serves to commit to the analysis plan outlined above. However, this study is part of a three-year funded research project by the first author. The study design, hypotheses and analysis plan are in line with the research proposal submitted in February, 2019.  
Before beginning data collection in July of 2021, we ran a  pilot version with small samples (N = 4) of two-, three- and four-year-old children to evaluate the age-appropriateness of the task and our stimulus design. We document all pilots and the specific conclusions we drew from them in the supplemental material accompanying the manuscript.

table.existing_data_explanation:
PILOT DATA
We ran a pilot version with small samples (N = 4) of four- and five-year-old children (Total N = 8) to evaluate the age-appropriateness of the task and our stimulus design. We document all pilots and the specific conclusions we drew from them in the supplemental material accompanying the manuscript. 
FIRST DATA COLLECTED
At the time of preregistration data from 8 participants has been collected. None of the data have been analysed at the time of preregistration.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Data collection will take place mostly in daycares from December 2021 to approximately June, 2022. All participants will be recruited in a medium-sized middle-European city, and come from a predominantly white population of middle to high income families. They are contacted via a database of participants for child development studies to which their parents had voluntarily signed up. Appointments are made on the basis of parents’ and children’s availability. 

Prior to the main study phase, children are tested with familiarization trials in which they simply have to point to the position of an item that was hidden in plain sight. This serves to ensure that children are comfortable and understand the task. In order to enter the main study phase, children should have a success rate of 66% in the familiarization. The experimenter provides at least four trials. If three in four are correct (75%), the child proceeds to the main phase. If not, two additional familiarization trials are run. If the child is correct in four out of six trials (66%), she proceeds to the main study phase. If not, two additional trials are presented. If six in eight are correct (75%), the child enters the main study phase. If children do not fulfill the criterion in a maximum of eight trials, they are dropped from the sample. Children will also be excluded from the sample if they do not provide at least 10 valid out of 20 possible trials in the main study phase. Trials are excluded if children do not respond, if responses cannot be interpreted, if parents or caregivers interfere with the procedure, or on the basis of technical problems or experimenter error.
table.sample_size_rationale: While using age as a continuous predictor is rare in developmental studies, we aim at having a sample of at least 24 children per year of age (two-, three-, and four-year-olds) which is in line with conventions in the field. This study is also a follow-up. The sample size has yielded reliable results in the context of highly similar design and analysis plans.
table.stopping_rule: In case children do not perform above chance as a group within the current age-range, the age-range will be extended by a year increasing the sample by 24 children until performance surpasses chance-level.
table.manipulated_variables: Children will be presented with an equal number of trials of all types of stimuli. Types of stimuli are not treated as different conditions (see analysis plan also).
table.measured_variables: The key dependent variable is children’s choice behavior in the object-choice-task. Choice items presented on the left and right side of a presentation screen. Children respond by pointing to the side of their choice. Children’s choices are coded as correct (1) or incorrect (0) in line with the logic of the task.

Development is a lasting change in the way a person perceives and deals with their environment. (Bronfenbrenner, 1979) Immersion in graphical systems of communication has profound consequences for perception and behavior (Dehaene, 2009; Dehaene et al., 2010).

text.text: Literacy acquisition -the process of learning to map meanings onto graphic forms -enhances meta-linguistic awareness (Olson, 2016), sharpens fine-grained visual discrimination (Duñabeitia et al., 2015), alters orientation processing (Fernandes et al., 2016), and shapes visual search strategies to align with reading direction (Woods et al., 2013).

text.text: But prior to reading words, children in industrialized societies are almost constantly surrounded by symbolic and graphical artifacts -such as arrowsthat they come to understand and use long before school age (Amsel & Byrnes, 2002).

text.text: The consequences of this constant but incidental type of enculturation on how children perceive symbolic artefacts are rarely studied -leaving open how children come to assign meaning to such symbols, which are among the first forms of graphic symbols they come to master.
Here we present three studies tracing the comprehension of arrows and markers throughout the preschool years.
Symbolic reference often relies on iconicity or convention, such as a pedestrian crossing sign depicting a human silhouette.
However, reference can also stem from spatio-temporal contiguity, as when a colored dot on an object signals ownership (Kanngiesser et al., 2019).
text.formatted: However, reference can also stem from spatio-temporal contiguity, as when a colored dot on an object signals ownership <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Kanngiesser et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Symbols grounded in physical contact, proximity, or directionality are known as deictic (Burks, 1949; Peirce, 1998).
text.formatted: Symbols grounded in physical contact, proximity, or directionality are known as deictic <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Burks, 1949;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Peirce, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: In face-to-face interaction, physical actions like touching or holding objects establish early joint attention (Tomasello, 2010) and underpin the development of pointing (O'Madagain et al., 2019; O'Madagain, 2027) -arguably human communication's most foundational form of reference.
text.formatted: In face-to-face interaction, physical actions like touching or holding objects establish early joint attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Tomasello, 2010)</ref> and underpin the development of pointing <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(O'Madagain et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">O'Madagain, 2027)</ref> -arguably human communication's most foundational form of reference.

text.text: In the graphic domain, markers and arrows serve as the visual analogues of touch and pointing.
Markers represent the more intuitive cue, relying purely on spatial proximity to a referent.

Arrows, by contrast, depend on convention: decoding them requires extrapolating an abstract vector from the arrowhead to a target -a interpretative process that is neither trivial (Jakobsen et al., 2013) nor inherent (Wittgenstein, 1953).
text.formatted: Arrows, by contrast, depend on convention: decoding them requires extrapolating an abstract vector from the arrowhead to a target -a interpretative process that is neither trivial <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Jakobsen et al., 2013)</ref> nor inherent <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Wittgenstein, 1953)</ref>.

text.text: Studies with children routinely rely on their ability to follow pointing gestures and physical markers, so the timeline of children's grasp of these cues is well understood.
In standard object-choice tasks, an experimenter hides a toy and indicates its location via pointing or placing a marker.
Successful choice requires children to process both the cue and their partner's helpful intent (Tomasello, 2010).
text.formatted: Successful choice requires children to process both the cue and their partner's helpful intent <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Tomasello, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Children succeed with pointing by 12 months (Behne et al., 2012; Sodian & Thoermer, 2004; Tomasello et al., 2007) and with physical markers by 18 months (Tomasello et al., 1997; Zlatev et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Children succeed with pointing by 12 months <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Behne et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Sodian & Thoermer, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Tomasello et al., 2007)</ref> and with physical markers by 18 months <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Tomasello et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Zlatev et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, developmental data on arrow-symbol comprehension remains scarce.

Studies report group-level success between ages two and three when arrows are held above targets (Leekam et al., 2010), between 30 and 36 months for printed arrows placed between choices (Jakobsen et al., 2013), and by age four for on-screen displays (Lee et al., 1998).
text.formatted: Studies report group-level success between ages two and three when arrows are held above targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Leekam et al., 2010)</ref>, between 30 and 36 months for printed arrows placed between choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Jakobsen et al., 2013)</ref>, and by age four for on-screen displays <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Lee et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: However, these studies fail to pinpoint success across the third year and suffer from a key ambiguity: placing the arrowhead closer to its target than a distractor cues the location via proximity as well as direction.
Consequently, it remains unclear whether young children understand arrows as vector symbols or merely markers.
In the case of finger-pointing, O'Madagain and colleagues (2019) pitted finger proximity to one location against directional alignment with another to disentangle these two possible interpretations.
text.formatted: In the case of finger-pointing, <ref type="bibr">O'Madagain and colleagues (2019)</ref> pitted finger proximity to one location against directional alignment with another to disentangle these two possible interpretations.

text.text: Children aged 18 and 36 months favored targets cued by proximity, six-year-olds were indecisive, and only nine-year-olds and adults consistently followed the vector (O' Madagain et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Children aged 18 and 36 months favored targets cued by proximity, six-year-olds were indecisive, and only nine-year-olds and adults consistently followed the vector (O' <ref type="bibr">Madagain et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This indicates that strict vector extrapolation is a mature strategy, and raises the possibility that understanding arrows as vector symbols is similarly late-developing.
Attentional cueing studies often contrast gaze and arrows as prototypical natural and conventional cues (Ciardo et al., 2019; Ristic et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Attentional cueing studies often contrast gaze and arrows as prototypical natural and conventional cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Ciardo et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Ristic et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: A common aim is to test whether arrows guide attention due to a conceptual decoding of their direction (endogenous cueing), or rather a perceptual response to visual asymmetry (exogenous cueing) as arrowheads arguably carry more perceptual weight than their shafts (Colombo, 2001; Jakobsen et al., 2013).
text.formatted: A common aim is to test whether arrows guide attention due to a conceptual decoding of their direction (endogenous cueing), or rather a perceptual response to visual asymmetry (exogenous cueing) as arrowheads arguably carry more perceptual weight than their shafts <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Colombo, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Jakobsen et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Isolating directional meaning from physical weight using variations of weighted as well as balanced double-headed arrows, Jakobsen and colleagues (2013) found that infants and 3-to 4-year-olds are driven by visual weight, whereas 5-to 6-year-olds and adults follow vector directions.

text.text: They concluded that children properly understand arrows as vector symbols no sooner than five years of age (see Supplementary Figure 1 for an overview of stimulus arrangements used in the studies reported above).
text.formatted: They concluded that children properly understand arrows as vector symbols no sooner than five years of age (see Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for an overview of stimulus arrangements used in the studies reported above).

text.text: From six years onward, perceptual cueing via arrows triggers reflexive orienting comparable to gaze -even when cues are uninformative, presented briefly, or despite explicit instructions to the contrary (Ciardo et al., 2019; Hommel et al., 2001; Senju et al., 2004; Wainwright & Bryson, 2005).
text.formatted: From six years onward, perceptual cueing via arrows triggers reflexive orienting comparable to gaze -even when cues are uninformative, presented briefly, or despite explicit instructions to the contrary <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Ciardo et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Hommel et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Senju et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Wainwright & Bryson, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: By school age, arrow-following is so deeply ingrained that it is considered overlearned.

That is, the processing of this conventional and acquired cue has become fully automatic and reflexive -reminiscent of developmental processes in literacy acquisition (Dehaene, 2009; Dehaene et al., 2010).
text.formatted: That is, the processing of this conventional and acquired cue has become fully automatic and reflexive -reminiscent of developmental processes in literacy acquisition <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dehaene, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Dehaene et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, existing developmental accounts leave open whether proximity or vector direction drives arrow interpretation in younger children, and precisely when a mature directional interpretation takes precedence.

Since only orientation can be understood as a genuine abstract interpretation of the arrow, while proximity is a 'natural' feature of the graphic element, the transition between proximity and orientation gives us a way to check at what age children's ability to apply abstract meanings to graphic elements truly begins.
To address this, the three studies presented below smoothly trace the development of graphical deixis across the preschool years employing novel stimulus configurations.
Study 1 tests spontaneous arrow comprehension free of spatial proximity or perceptual-weight confounds, while contrasting performance directly with graphic markers.

Study 2 disentangles the competing roles of spatial proximity and vector direction in children's interpretation of arrows by presenting ambiguous displays, and Study 3 pioneers a set of novel vector symbols to demonstrate when preschoolers productively generalize the vector principle to unfamiliar instances.

The objectchoice paradigm employed in all three studies goes beyond attentional cueing and requires children to actively interpret and respond to these cues under conditions of minimal instruction and without feedback.

To trace the onset of children's comprehension of arrows and markers, Study 1 tested children between 2 and 5 years of age using a picture-book-style object-choice task in which a cartoon agent was providing a marker or simplified arrow to guide children's choices.

Based on the literature (Leekam et al., 2010; Tomasello et al., 1997; Zlatev et al., 2013), we derived the hypotheses that children would succeed earlier in the Marker condition than in the Arrow condition (H1), but would perform above chance in both conditions by age four (H2).
text.formatted: Based on the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Leekam et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Tomasello et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Zlatev et al., 2013)</ref>, we derived the hypotheses that children would succeed earlier in the Marker condition than in the Arrow condition (H1), but would perform above chance in both conditions by age four (H2).

text.text: To achieve dense, continuous sampling we tested two children per month of age between the second and fifth birthday.
The final sample comprised 72 children (𝑀 = 41.47 months, 𝑆𝐷 = 10.50 months, range 24 -59 months; 36 female).
All participants came from a predominantly white population of middle to high income families and were recruited in [MASKED FOR REVIEW], a major European city.
Parents were invited via a database of participants for child development studies for which they had signed up.
Children were tested in day-and after schoolcare for the most part, and occasionally in the lab or at home.

In addition, 12 children were tested but not submitted to the final sample for not fulfilling the preregistered criteria of succeeding during familiarization (𝑁 = 7, see below), or because they did not finish a minimum of 8 test trials (𝑁 = 2).
Furthermore, 3 children were excluded due to being fussy during testing.
Data collection took place between July 2021 and April 2022.
Tasks were presented on a screen in the style of an interactive picture-book (cf.
Figure 1 A).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> A).

text.text: To introduce the game, the experimenter (E) presented a cartoon monkey (Coco) who placed a banana under one of two cups in plain sight.
Children were asked, "Where is the banana?"
and indicated their choice by pointing.
E provided immediate feedback ("Well done!"
or "Hmm, let's try again!") while revealing the banana in 4 to 8 total familiarization trials depending on whether the children chose correctly or needed more training.
After familiarization, E announced that the monkey wanted to play a new game where they could not know the banana's location.
An occluder covered the lower half of the screen, obscuring the hiding process.
E narrated, "Coco is going to help you find the banana,".
As soon as the monkey placed a marker or arrow to guide children's choice, they were prompted "Where is the banana?".
E provided no feedback during test trials and merely acknowledged responses with a neutral "Thank you!".
Children were neither instructed to follow cues nor did E describe the cues as markers or arrows.
Trial presentations lasted 20-30 seconds.
Children completed up to 16 test trials -8 per conditionadding up to a 5-10 minute session per participant.
The order of conditions was blocked and counterbalanced across participants as was the side of the target.
To be included in the analysis, children were required to succeed in at least 66% of familiarization trials, and to complete a minimum of eight valid test trials.
In the Marker Condition, the monkey placed a circle directly on either hiding place, akin to a sticker covering the target partially (see Figure 1 B).
text.formatted: In the Marker Condition, the monkey placed a circle directly on either hiding place, akin to a sticker covering the target partially (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1 B</ref>).

text.text: In the Arrow Condition, the monkey placed an equilateral triangle in the bottom center of the screen, with one vertex directed at either the left or right target (Figure 1 C).
text.formatted: In the Arrow Condition, the monkey placed an equilateral triangle in the bottom center of the screen, with one vertex directed at either the left or right target (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1 C</ref>).

In three complementary studies we tested young children in picture-book-style symbolic object-choice-tasks to investigate their comprehension of markers, arrows and novel vector symbols.
Study 1 established that children are capable of reading markers and arrows in the context of graphic displays at about 35 months of age.
These findings contradict the presumption that only five-year-olds begin to grasp the conceptual meaning of arrows (Jakobsen et al., 2013).
text.formatted: These findings contradict the presumption that only five-year-olds begin to grasp the conceptual meaning of arrows <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Jakobsen et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: As the study employed a reduced arrow cue lacking visual weight, results cannot be explained by exogenous cueing and low-level visual features.
Rather, we find children to be able to follow directional cues in the absence of visual weight and proximity confounds just before their third birthday.
In Study 2, children completed tasks with either redundant or competing displays of arrow cues, where spatial proximity and vector direction aligned or conflicted.
Here our goal was to understand at what age children prioritize the orientation of the symbol -the abstract content, that is -when proximity would predict a different target.

In congruent cases, effects of proximity and direction generally added up, but children succeeded basically at the same ages in the Congruent condition as in the Marker and Arrow conditions of Study 1, which may be indicative of a developmental threshold: children just master dual representation at the end of the third year (DeLoache, 2011) and may not be able to succeed earlier when tested with deictic symbols in the graphic domain.

text.text: The Incongruent condition yielded a remarkable developmental pattern: up to three and a half years children favored a proximity-based interpretation of the stimulus and systematically ignored pointing direction.

Performance improved strongly between the fourth and fifth birthday and -by five years of age -extrapolating a vector from an arrow appears to be so internalized and habitual that children systematically ignored conflicting proximity cues leading to stable above-chance performance from 59 months onward.

These results are in line with analogical results in the comprehension of the pointing gesture: children were found to overcome a proximity bias, and interpret pointing gestures purely in terms of their orientation, only after six years of age (O'Madagain et al., 2019).

text.text: The results from the Incongruent condition indicate a strong change in the way young children spontaneously structure an ambiguous graphic array, switching from favoring a proximity-based interpretation driven by salience and perceptual grouping to a vector-based interpretation resting on an abstract cultural norm.

Accordingly, we interpret these results to document the emergence of a specific form of visual expertise in the graphic domain that mirrors effects of literacy acquisition (Dehaene, 2009; Dehaene et al., 2010), but emerges significantly earlier.

text.text: Our preferred interpretation is that children around three and a half years of age have sufficiently internalized the principle of vector symbols that they systematically read such novel displays as arrows.

With the exception of the use of a texture gradient in an attentional cueing paradigm (Brignani et al., 2009), this is the first time an experimental manipulation investigated children's proficiency with deictic symbols on cues that are not resembling conventional arrows, pointing gestures or gaze.

text.text: Together, our findings show a clear developmental trajectory in the interpretation of graphic deixis.
Children read both arrows and markers by the end of their third year -coinciding with the onset of representational insight (DeLoache, 2011).

text.text: However, both proximity and orientation can play a role in fixing the reference of these symbols.
When these two referential principles conflict, children favor marker-based proximity up to 3.5 years; however, throughout the fourth year, this preference shifts toward directionality.

Already at this stage, vectorprojection is not restricted to conventional arrows, but serves as a productive semiotic principle that children spontaneously apply to novel symbols in relevant contexts.
By the fifth year, the vector-based interpretation of directional cues becomes so deeply ingrained that it dominates even against competing spatial evidence.
We propose that growing up immersed in graphic environments fosters perceptual habits and symbolic expertise that lead children to treat specific graphic cues as inherently directional.
Future research should directly track individual exposure to graphic symbols and provide cross-cultural comparisons in less graphically saturated contexts.

Methodologically, key next steps include testing whether these proximity-vector trade-offs extend to 3D physical spaces (O'Madagain et al., 2019) and using eye-tracking to capture realtime attentional allocation under cue conflict.

The Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC) for the full (WAIC = 1,118.43) and the reduced model (WAIC = 1116) are almost identical.

Comparing weights based on the WAIC yielded 0% of the model weight for the full model, and 100% for the reduced model, strongly favoring the simpler model lacking the interaction of age and condition.

At the same time, comparison of the models' WAIC using expected log predictive density (ELPD) shows that this difference is not statistically meaningful (ELPD WAIC; full model = -559.21; reduced model = -558).
The standard error of the difference in predictive accuracy (𝑆𝐸 = 0.50) shows that the difference itself (ELPD diff = -1.21) is negligible.
In the absence of conclusive evidence for either model, we report estimates from the full model in line with the preregistration.

Analyses in Study 2 followed the same rationale as in Study 1 and compared the performance of a full model (𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑡 ∼ 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 * 𝑐. 𝑎𝑔𝑒 + 𝑐. 𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑙 + 𝑠𝑒𝑥 + (𝑐. 𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑙 | 𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑖𝑑)) with a reduced model lacking the interaction of condition and age (𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑡 ∼ 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 + 𝑐. 𝑎𝑔𝑒 + 𝑐. 𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑙 + 𝑠𝑒𝑥 + (𝑐. 𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑙 | 𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑖𝑑)).

Effective sample sizes for all fixed effects in the full model (Bulk ESS, 𝑀 = 6741, range 2433 -16200) and the reduced model (Bulk ESS, 𝑀 =5573, range 1975-10819) were >1000, indicating reliable posterior estimations.

The gain in fit resulting from including an interaction of age and condition justifies the additional complexity.
This is corroborated by comparing weights based on the WAIC: the full model gains 97.56% of the model weight, whereas only 2.44% of the weight is allocated to the reduced model.

Finally, a comparison of the models' WAIC via ELPD shows that the difference (ELPD diff = -54.24) is much larger than its standard error (𝑆𝐸 = 9.85), showing that the full model would predict out of sample data much more accurately.
